question: What first drew you to journalism as something you want to study?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin for the interest rather than a vague love of writing or talking to people.

bullets: Name a concrete moment, story, or piece of work that pulled you in
Explain what it revealed about what journalism actually does
Connect it to something you've done since, not just admired
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I got hooked in Year 11 when our local paper ran an investigation into overcrowding at a nearby care home, and I watched conditions actually change within weeks of publication. It was the first time I understood that reporting isn't just describing the world, it can move it. I started writing for my school newspaper right after, and I've been chasing that same feeling of a story that does something ever since.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I've always loved writing' with no specific story or moment
Describing journalism as glamorous without mentioning the work involved
Giving an answer that could apply to English or Communications just as easily
followUps: What has your own writing or reporting shown you that surprised you?

question: Why journalism specifically, rather than English literature or a general communications degree?
lookingFor: A clear sense of what makes journalism distinct: verification, deadlines, public accountability, not just skilled writing.

bullets: Distinguish journalism's core discipline (facts, sourcing, deadlines) from creative or general communication
Show awareness that journalism serves a public accountability function
Ground it in something practical you've tried, like reporting a real story
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I considered English because I do love writing, but journalism is really about a different discipline, you're accountable to what actually happened, not just to a good sentence. When I reported on our school's cancelled bus route for the student paper, I had to check three different accounts before I trusted the story, and that verification process is what I find genuinely interesting, not just telling stories well but earning the right to tell them. Communications felt too broad for what I want, which is specifically the reporting and truth-checking side.

commonMistakes: Treating journalism as just 'writing but for news'
Dismissing English or Communications rather than explaining the distinction
No mention of verification, sourcing, or accountability
followUps: What's the difference between reporting and storytelling, in your view?

question: Why do you want to study journalism at our university specifically?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this program's features, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific feature: a newsroom placement, a faculty member, a student publication, a broadcast studio
Connect it to a concrete gap in what you've done so far
Show you understand what makes this program different from others you could apply to
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your program is one of very few that guarantees a placement at a partner newsroom in second year, and that hands-on requirement is exactly what I'm missing right now, I've written plenty but never worked inside an actual editorial process with a real deadline and an editor pushing back. I also read about your student-run investigative unit, which broke a story on university housing conditions last year, and that's the kind of work I want to be part of, not just observe. It felt like the program treats journalism as a practice you do, not just a subject you study.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that would apply to any journalism course
Citing rankings instead of specific program features
Confusing this program with a different school's media studies course
followUps: What would you want to work on if you got that placement?

question: Is there a news story you've read or watched that made you think, that's the kind of journalism I want to do?
lookingFor: Specific engagement with a real piece of journalism and an articulate reason it resonated.

bullets: Name an actual story or reporter, not a vague genre
Explain what the reporting technique or impact was, not just the topic
Connect it to the kind of work you'd want to produce
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It was a local investigation into a hospital trust missing its own safety targets, built almost entirely from freedom of information requests rather than leaks or interviews. What struck me was how patient the reporting was, months of document requests before a single paragraph got written, and the story held up because of that groundwork. It made me want to do the unglamorous part of journalism well, the data requests and record-checking, because that's clearly where the real accountability comes from.

commonMistakes: Naming a topic instead of an actual piece of journalism
Praising a story only for being 'interesting' with no sense of craft
Picking something purely for shock value with no reflection
followUps: What would you have done differently if you'd reported that story?

question: What do you read or watch to keep up with the news, and why those sources?
lookingFor: A deliberate, varied news diet with some reasoning about source reliability, not a single app checked passively.

bullets: Name specific outlets across at least two formats or perspectives
Explain why you chose that mix, not just that you consume news
Show some awareness of each source's strengths or limitations
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read a national broadsheet every morning for the agenda-setting stories, but I also follow two local papers because I think that's where journalism's accountability role is most visible and most under threat right now. I listen to a couple of long-form podcasts for context that a daily article can't give, and I try to read at least one outlet I disagree with politically, just to notice how differently the same story gets framed. It's less about any one source being right and more about triangulating.

commonMistakes: Naming only social media or a single app with no critical reflection
Claiming to read 'everything' with no specifics
Only naming sources that confirm one political viewpoint
followUps: Can you think of a story that two of those outlets covered very differently?

question: Is there a journalist whose work you admire? What is it about their reporting that stands out to you?
lookingFor: Specific, substantive knowledge of a real journalist's work, not just a famous name dropped for effect.

bullets: Name a specific journalist and a specific piece of their work
Identify a concrete craft element you admire, not just their fame
Show you've thought about how that influences your own approach
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I admire Katherine Boo's work, particularly her book on a Mumbai slum, because she spent years embedded before writing a word, and it shows in how she lets people's own contradictions sit on the page instead of flattening them into a simple narrative. What I take from that is patience, resisting the urge to file the easy version of a story before you've actually understood it. It's shaped how I try to approach even small local stories, going back for a second and third conversation rather than settling for the first quote.

commonMistakes: Naming a celebrity anchor with no discussion of their actual reporting
Vague praise like 'they're really good' with no specifics
Choosing someone purely because they seem like the expected answer
followUps: What would you want to borrow from their approach, and what would you do differently?

question: Tell us about a piece of journalism you've produced, for a school paper, blog, podcast, or elsewhere.
lookingFor: Real hands-on experience with a specific example, showing understanding of process, not just the finished product.

bullets: Describe a specific piece: the topic, the reporting process, and the outcome
Mention a concrete challenge you had to solve while producing it
Reflect honestly on what you'd improve
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wrote a piece for my school's newsletter about why our canteen switched suppliers, and the hard part was that the school wouldn't confirm anything on the record at first. I ended up finding the change logged in public council catering tender documents, which let me write the story accurately without relying on an official statement I wasn't getting. Looking back, I'd have pushed harder for a direct quote from the head, because the piece leaned too heavily on documents and not enough on voices.

commonMistakes: Describing only the topic with no detail on the actual reporting process
Overselling a minor piece as if it were a major investigation
No honest reflection on what could have been done better
followUps: What would you have done if the documents hadn't been available?

question: What makes a story newsworthy? How would you decide what goes on the front page today?
lookingFor: Awareness of basic news values (timeliness, impact, proximity, prominence, conflict) applied with real judgement.

bullets: Name a few actual news values, not just 'if it's interesting'
Show these values are weighed against each other, not applied mechanically
Give a concrete example to illustrate the trade-off
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think about it as a mix of impact, how many people it actually affects, proximity, how close it is to the audience, and timeliness. But those pull against each other constantly, a distant disaster with huge impact often has to compete with a smaller local story that matters more directly to your specific readers. If I were choosing a front page, I'd ask which story most changes what my readers need to know or do tomorrow, and that's usually the local story most people would otherwise miss entirely.

commonMistakes: Reducing newsworthiness to 'whatever gets the most clicks'
Naming values with no sense of how they compete with each other
No real example to test the reasoning
followUps: How would your answer change for a story that's important but not urgent?

question: What's the difference between a news report and an opinion piece, and why does that distinction matter?
lookingFor: Clear grasp of the basic separation between reporting and commentary, and why blurring it damages trust.

bullets: State the core difference: news reports facts and events, opinion pieces argue a position
Note that opinion should be clearly labelled and still fact-based
Explain why confusing the two erodes reader trust
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A news report tells readers what happened, sourced and verified, while an opinion piece argues a particular interpretation or position, ideally one still grounded in facts rather than invented ones. The distinction matters because readers need to know whether they're being told what happened or being persuaded of something, and when outlets blur that line, readers stop trusting either category. I think that's actually one of journalism's biggest current problems, opinion dressed up as reporting.

commonMistakes: Saying opinion pieces don't need to be factual at all
Treating the distinction as unimportant or old-fashioned
Confusing analysis, which is reported and labelled, with straight opinion
followUps: Where would you place analysis pieces on that spectrum?

question: Can a journalist ever be truly objective? How would you handle your own biases when reporting a story?
lookingFor: A mature, realistic view of objectivity as a discipline of process rather than a claim of having no viewpoint.

bullets: Acknowledge that complete neutrality is unrealistic, everyone has a perspective
Reframe objectivity as a method: fairness, verification, seeking out opposing views
Give or imagine a concrete practice for checking your own bias
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think anyone reports from nowhere, everyone brings assumptions, so I see objectivity less as having no opinion and more as a discipline, deliberately seeking out the strongest version of views I don't hold and checking my own facts as hard as I'd check anyone else's. When I wrote about a proposed bike lane near my house, which I personally wanted, I made myself interview two shopkeepers who opposed it and let their strongest argument actually appear in the piece, not just a token line. That process, not some claim of neutrality, is what I think makes reporting trustworthy.

commonMistakes: Claiming to have no opinions or biases at all
Concluding that objectivity is impossible so it's not worth trying for
No concrete method for managing personal bias
followUps: What would you do if you realised, partway through a story, that your own bias had shaped your questions?

question: You've heard a striking claim from one source. What steps would you take before you'd feel comfortable publishing it?
lookingFor: A basic but genuine verification instinct, corroboration, checking documents, contacting the subject.

bullets: Insist on at least a second independent source before publishing
Mention checking any available documents or records
Include giving the subject of the claim a chance to respond
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One source alone wouldn't be enough for me, I'd want at least one more person or a document that corroborates it independently, not just someone who heard the same rumour. If it's a claim about a specific person or organisation, I'd also go to them directly for a response before publishing, because that's both fair and often reveals whether the claim actually holds up. Only once I had that second layer of confirmation would I feel the story was solid enough to run.

commonMistakes: Saying they'd publish based on one source if it 'sounds credible'
Forgetting to seek a response from the person or organisation named
No mention of documentary corroboration where it exists
followUps: What would you do if the second source contradicted the first?

question: A source will only talk to you if you grant them anonymity, and the information is important. How would you decide whether to agree?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning about when anonymity is justified, and awareness of the obligations it creates.

bullets: Weigh the public interest of the information against the risk of unverifiable claims
Recognise that granting anonymity creates a commitment you must honour
Note the need to still corroborate the claim independently, not just take it on trust
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by asking why they need anonymity, whistleblowers with real risk to their job or safety are a very different case from someone who just wants to avoid accountability for what they're saying. If the information genuinely serves the public interest and I can't get it any other way, I'd agree, but I'd still try to corroborate it independently rather than running purely on their word. And once I'd given that promise, I'd treat it as absolute, because breaking it doesn't just harm that source, it damages every future source's trust in me.

commonMistakes: Granting anonymity automatically whenever a source asks
Treating an anonymous claim as verified simply because the source seems credible
Not recognising anonymity as a binding, ongoing commitment
followUps: What would you do if an editor later pressured you to reveal the source?

question: You're assigned to cover a story involving a club or organisation you're personally a member of. What would you do?
lookingFor: Recognition of conflict of interest and a concrete plan for handling it, not just good intentions.

bullets: Recognise the conflict of interest explicitly rather than assuming personal fairness is enough
Disclose the connection to an editor before proceeding
Consider stepping back from the story if the conflict is significant enough to undermine trust
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct might be that I can just be fair despite the connection, but I don't think that's good enough, readers can't see my intentions, only the byline and the affiliation. I'd disclose the conflict to my editor straight away and let them decide whether I should still cover it, and if I did, I'd disclose the connection in the piece itself so readers can judge for themselves. If the story involved something serious, like wrongdoing inside that organisation, I'd actually push to be taken off it entirely, because the appearance of a conflict can undermine a story as much as an actual one.

commonMistakes: Assuming personal fairness resolves the conflict without disclosure
Hiding the connection rather than raising it with an editor
Treating disclosure alone as sufficient in every case, regardless of severity
followUps: Would your answer change if you were the only reporter available to cover it?

question: A dramatic video is going viral on social media claiming to show a breaking event. How would you verify it before reporting on it?
lookingFor: Practical digital verification instinct, geolocation, reverse image search, cross-referencing, not blind trust in virality.

bullets: Treat virality itself as no evidence of authenticity
Mention concrete verification steps like reverse image search or checking metadata and location details
Cross-check against other independent accounts or official sources before reporting
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The fact that something is spreading fast tells me nothing about whether it's real, if anything it makes me more cautious, because misinformation spreads exactly the same way. I'd try a reverse image search to see if the footage has appeared before under a different story, check details in the video like signage, weather, or shadows against the claimed location and time, and look for any independent accounts corroborating it. Only once at least one of those checks held up would I consider reporting on it, and even then I'd be careful to attribute it clearly as unverified footage if certainty wasn't fully possible.

commonMistakes: Treating high view counts or shares as a sign of credibility
No concrete verification technique mentioned
Reporting the video immediately to avoid being 'scooped'
followUps: What would you do if you couldn't verify it in time but competitors were already reporting it?

question: Why is press freedom important, and can you think of a case where it was tested?
lookingFor: Understanding of press freedom as a democratic safeguard, backed by a real example, not just abstract praise.

bullets: Explain press freedom's role in holding power accountable
Cite a specific real case, historical or recent
Acknowledge press freedom comes with responsibility, not as an unlimited right
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Press freedom matters because it's often the only mechanism ordinary people have for finding out what powerful institutions would rather keep hidden, without it, wrongdoing has no real check on it. The Pentagon Papers case is the one that sticks with me, a newspaper published classified documents showing the government had misled the public about a war, and the courts ultimately backed the paper's right to publish. That said, I don't think press freedom means freedom from responsibility, it comes with an obligation to verify and to weigh genuine harm, which is part of what makes it a serious craft rather than a blank cheque.

commonMistakes: Only offering an abstract statement with no specific example
Treating press freedom as an unlimited right with no accompanying responsibility
Confusing press freedom with freedom of speech generally
followUps: Where do you think the line should sit between press freedom and national security concerns?

question: How has social media changed the way news is reported and consumed, in your view?
lookingFor: A balanced view that names both the benefits (speed, eyewitness access) and the risks (misinformation, erosion of gatekeeping).

bullets: Note the benefit: faster eyewitness reporting and access to underreported stories
Note the risk: misinformation spreads before verification can catch up
Reflect on what this means for a trained journalist's role today
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Social media means events now reach the public within minutes, often from people on the ground before any reporter arrives, which has genuinely surfaced stories that traditional gatekeepers used to miss. But that speed comes at a cost, false or misleading claims travel just as fast, sometimes faster, because there's no editorial check before something is shared. I think that actually raises the value of trained journalists rather than making us obsolete, someone still has to do the slower work of verifying what's true among everything that's circulating.

commonMistakes: Framing social media as purely negative for journalism
Framing it as purely positive with no mention of misinformation risk
No reflection on what it means for their own future role
followUps: Do you think traditional newsrooms have adapted well to this shift?

question: What's the key difference between journalism and public relations?
lookingFor: Clear grasp that journalism serves the public's right to know while PR serves a client's interests, with independence as the key marker.

bullets: State that PR represents and promotes a specific client or organisation
State that journalism aims for independent, verified reporting in the public interest
Note why confusing the two, or a lack of independence, damages credibility
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: PR exists to represent an organisation's interests and present them in the best light, which is a legitimate job but a fundamentally different one. Journalism's job is to report independently and let the facts land where they land, even when that's uncomfortable for the people being covered. The moment a journalist starts thinking like a PR representative for a source, protecting them rather than reporting on them fairly, that's when independence and public trust start to break down.

commonMistakes: Treating the two as basically interchangeable
Describing PR dismissively without explaining the actual functional difference
No mention of independence as the core distinction
followUps: How would you handle a press release that seems designed to bury a bad story?

question: How would you handle interviewing someone who is being evasive or won't answer your question directly?
lookingFor: Practical interviewing technique: persistence, rephrasing, follow-ups, without becoming hostile or giving up.

bullets: Stay calm and avoid turning the interview into a confrontation
Use follow-up and rephrased questions to return to the point
Know when to note the evasion itself as part of the story
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd try not to react with frustration, because that usually makes someone dig in further, so I'd calmly rephrase the question and come back to it from a different angle. If they kept sidestepping, I'd ask a very specific, narrow follow-up that's harder to deflect than the original open question. And if they still wouldn't answer, I think that's worth being honest about in the piece itself, noting plainly that the question was asked and not answered, because that's information too.

commonMistakes: Giving up on the question after one deflection
Becoming aggressive or confrontational instead of persistent
Not considering that the evasion itself can be reported
followUps: How would your approach differ interviewing a grieving family member versus a public official?

question: You're sent to cover a tragedy where local families have lost loved ones. How do you balance getting the story with treating people with care?
lookingFor: Genuine empathy paired with professional judgement, showing the two aren't in conflict.

bullets: Reject the false choice between compassion and good reporting
Describe concrete practices: asking permission, respecting a no, giving people time
Explain why respectful reporting also tends to produce more honest, better material
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think care and getting the story are actually opposed, if anything, treating people with respect tends to get you a truer, more honest interview than pushing hard ever would. I'd always ask before approaching someone rather than assuming they want to talk, accept a no without pressing further, and let them set the pace of the conversation rather than rushing for a quote. It's also just the right way to treat people who are having the worst day of their lives, regardless of what it does for the story.

commonMistakes: Prioritising getting the quote over the person's wellbeing
Framing empathy and good reporting as fundamentally in tension
No concrete practice, just a vague claim of being sensitive
followUps: What would you do if a family member later asked you to remove something they'd said?

question: You realise, after publication, that a fact in your story was wrong. What do you do?
lookingFor: Prompt, transparent correction and ownership, not defensiveness or quietly editing the piece.

bullets: Correct it quickly rather than hoping no one notices
Be transparent about the correction rather than silently editing the piece
Reflect on what in the process let the error through, to prevent repeats
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd flag it to my editor immediately and get a correction published as soon as possible, because sitting on it only makes it worse. I wouldn't just quietly fix the text either, I'd add a clear correction note so readers can see exactly what changed and why, because pretending it never happened undermines trust more than the original mistake did. Afterwards I'd want to go back and figure out where my verification process broke down, so the same kind of error doesn't happen again.

commonMistakes: Quietly editing the article with no visible correction
Delaying the correction out of embarrassment
Treating it as a one-off with no reflection on process
followUps: What would you do differently if the error had already caused real harm to someone's reputation?

question: Are you more drawn to local reporting or national or international journalism? Why?
lookingFor: A genuine preference backed by reasoning, showing understanding of what each level of journalism actually involves.

bullets: State a genuine preference, not a hedge that avoids committing
Explain what specifically draws them to that scale of reporting
Show awareness of the different skills or trade-offs each involves
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm drawn to local reporting, honestly, because it's where I've seen journalism have the most direct, visible effect, a story about our council's spending decisions actually changed something within a month, in a way a national story rarely does that quickly. National journalism has huge reach and resources I find appealing too, but local reporting means you're accountable to people you'll actually run into at the shop the next day, which I think keeps you honest in a very particular way. I'd love to end up covering local government or education specifically.

commonMistakes: Refusing to commit to a preference at all
Dismissing local journalism as a lesser stepping stone rather than valuable in itself
No specific reasoning behind the stated preference
followUps: What's a local story in your own area that you think deserves more coverage?

question: Journalism today often involves more than writing, video, audio, social posting, data visuals. Which of those are you keen to develop, and why?
lookingFor: Realistic self-assessment of current skills plus genuine interest in developing new ones, not just claiming to be an expert at everything.

bullets: Name a specific format honestly, including current skill level
Explain why that format appeals or fits the kind of story they want to tell
Show awareness that different stories suit different formats
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm confident in writing, that's where I've done most of my practice, but audio is what I actually want to develop next. I did a short interview-based podcast episode for a school project and found that hearing someone's actual voice and pauses carries emotion that text sometimes flattens out. I think some stories, especially personal ones, are better told that way, so I'd like to get properly trained in editing and structuring audio rather than treating it as an afterthought.

commonMistakes: Claiming expert-level skill in every format with no honest self-assessment
Dismissing formats other than writing as unimportant
No reasoning for why a particular format appeals to them
followUps: Can you think of a story that would work better as text than as video, or vice versa?

question: What role do you think journalism plays in a functioning democracy?
lookingFor: A substantive answer beyond 'informing the public', touching on accountability, agenda-setting, or the watchdog function.

bullets: Go beyond 'informing people' to name a specific function, such as accountability or agenda-setting
Give a concrete example illustrating that function
Show awareness of the tension when trust in journalism itself is declining
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Beyond just informing people, I think journalism's core democratic function is accountability, it's often the only institution whose job is specifically to check what power is doing and tell the public, outside of elections themselves. The care home investigation I mentioned earlier is a small example, but it's the same mechanism at a national scale, reporting that forces a response because it's made public. What worries me is that trust in journalism has fallen in a lot of places, which weakens that whole mechanism, and I think that's actually one of the more urgent problems for the field right now.

commonMistakes: Stopping at a generic 'informs the public' with no deeper function named
No concrete example to ground the claim
Ignoring the current pressures on public trust in journalism
followUps: What do you think journalism could do to rebuild public trust?

subtopic: A story they would want to investigate
question: If you could investigate any story right now, with full resources and time, what would it be?
lookingFor: Genuine curiosity backed by a plausible reporting plan, showing they've thought about how, not just what.

bullets: Name a specific, well-defined story rather than a broad topic
Sketch a realistic starting point: documents, sources, or data
Explain why this particular story matters to them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to look into how student mental health referral waiting lists are actually managed behind the scenes, because everyone talks about the crisis but I've never seen anyone show exactly where in the process the delays happen. I'd start with freedom of information requests to local health boards for the actual referral and waiting time data, then try to find families willing to walk me through their own case timeline against those numbers. It matters to me because I've watched friends wait months with no real explanation, and I think the story is less about the crisis existing, which people already know, and more about exactly where the system breaks.

commonMistakes: Naming a topic so broad it isn't really a story
No sense of where they'd actually start reporting it
Choosing something purely dramatic with no personal or reasoned connection
followUps: What's the biggest obstacle you'd expect to hit reporting that story?

question: Journalists often face public criticism, or even hostility, for stories they've published. How would you cope with that?
lookingFor: Realistic resilience: distinguishing fair criticism worth acting on from noise, without becoming either defensive or thin-skinned.

bullets: Show they understand criticism comes with the job, not as an unfair surprise
Describe how they'd separate legitimate criticism from bad-faith attacks
Give or imagine a concrete example of taking feedback seriously
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd expect it, honestly, if a story has any real impact, someone affected by it is probably not going to be happy about it. What I'd try to do is separate genuine, specific criticism, someone pointing out an actual factual issue, from people who are just angry about being covered at all, and take the first kind seriously every time. When a source I quoted in a school piece felt I'd taken their comment out of context, I went back and reread the full recording, and I had trimmed it in a way that changed the meaning slightly, so I corrected it, and that experience taught me to slow down more with quotes generally.

commonMistakes: Claiming criticism never bothers them at all, sounding unrealistic
Treating all criticism as illegitimate or an attack
No concrete example of actually learning from feedback
followUps: How would you handle it differently if the criticism came from your own editor rather than the public?
